description: Structured glaze/body defect troubleshooting, sourced from Digitalfire's Troubles pages ahead of the site's shutdown. Intended to replace the predictor's explicitly-labeled 'heuristic estimates not calibrated against firing data' with published cause/cure reasoning.

crazing.summary: Fine surface cracks. The fired glaze has a significantly higher coefficient of thermal expansion than the body - no amount of careful firing or thin application avoids it once the mismatch is real.
crazing.chemistry_cause: Excess high-expansion oxides, chiefly K2O and Na2O.
chemistry_remedies: Replace K2O/Na2O with lower-expansion fluxes: MgO, CaO, ZnO
Introduce B2O3 to replace some of the alkali flux
Increase SiO2 in glossy, well-melted glazes (raises Si:Al but lowers expansion)
Add enough flux to allow more SiO2 and Al2O3 - both are very low expansion
other_remedies: Use 325 mesh silica instead of 200 mesh for better melt dissolution
Adjust the clay body itself: add talc or dolomite to raise body expansion to meet the glaze
Add zirconium opacifier (up to ~3%) to slightly reduce expansion
Substitute a lower-expansion frit, especially where frit is 30%+ of the recipe

cross_reference.note: Corroborates the Digitalfire remedies (add silica/talc). Also notes crazing can be deliberately induced for a controlled test: replace potash feldspar with soda feldspar or nepheline syenite, or reduce silica in 5% increments.

shivering.summary: The opposite of crazing: the glaze is under compression and flakes off the body, especially at edges. Glaze tolerates compression far worse than tension, so shivering is less common but more dangerous - flakes can be razor-sharp, a food-safety hazard.
shivering.chemistry_cause: Glaze COE too low relative to the body COE.
chemistry_remedies: Raise glaze expansion by substituting some CaO/MgO/Li2O/SrO/ZnO for Na2O
Switch to a higher-sodium frit (e.g. Ferro 3110)
Change only the Na2O/K2O balance when adjusting via chemistry software, compensating for any other oxides a feldspar or frit swap would introduce

cross_reference.note: Remedy: add 5% nepheline syenite, or reduce silica by 5%.

crawling.summary: Molten glaze withdraws into islands, leaving bare clay patches.
causes: Excessive drying shrinkage from too much raw clay in the glaze (over ~20% ball clay/kaolin)
Poor glaze-to-bisque bond
Slow drying (thick walls, dense bisque, high water content) that prolongs the fragile pre-crack stage
remedies: Replace some high-plasticity clay (ball clay) with a less plastic kaolin
Calcine part of the clay content - e.g. 35% kaolin as 15% calcined + 20% raw
Check specific gravity of the slurry; use deflocculant/flocculant to correct
Add gum binder to harden the dried layer and bond it to bisque
Apply thinner layers; a fountain-glazing approach for interiors
Speed drying: preheat bisque before dipping, thinner coats, more porous (lower-fired) bisque
Replace Gerstley Borate with a boron frit; use calcined rather than raw zinc oxide
For multi-coat glazes: make the upper layer lower-clay/lower-shrinkage, apply thin and fast-drying, or bisque between coats

cross_reference.note: To deliberately induce (for testing): replace dolomite with light magnesium carbonate and apply the glaze more thickly. To prevent: apply more thinly, reduce clay content, or sponge the bisque clean before glazing.

pinholing_pitting.summary: Small holes or pits where escaping gas disrupted the melt before it could heal over.

body: Large or gas-producing particles that decompose late
Particles that melt too vigorously, forming glass chemistry that resists healing
Talc/dolomite/whiting release large gas volumes during decomposition
Soluble salts migrating to the surface on drying, forming a reactive layer
Open/porous body structure venting gas faster than the glaze can heal
Immature (underfired) body robbing the glaze of flux
Rough bisque surface from grog, sand, or trimming marks
glaze: Late-decomposing materials (whiting, dolomite, talc, coloring carbonates) still gassing after the glaze starts to melt
Standard glaze fired on a fast-fire schedule it was not formulated for
Viscous melt that resists gas bubbles passing through
Glaze sealing over before the body finishes outgassing
application: Too-thin application with insufficient glaze to heal disruptions
Excessive slurry water, poor bonding, trapped air
firing: Firing too rapidly for the melt to smooth over disruptions
Mismatched gas-evolution timing between body and glaze
Uneven heating (electric kiln, heavy or shaded ware)
Fast cooldown - pitting can occur on cooling too, especially with high-sulphur bodies

remedies: Sieve-analyze and replace coarse or gassy body particles
Substitute wollastonite for whiting (CaO), frits for MgO/talc, ceramic stains for carbonates
Bisque as high and as long as practical, with good oxidizing airflow
Slow the firing curve toward cone end (e.g. ~1 hour/cone at cone 6); soak if possible
Slow cool from peak - drop-and-hold, or ~150F/hr cooling through the critical range
Increase melt fluidity (more flux, lower Al2O3:SiO2, ZnO/SrO/Li2O additions) so bubbles can pass
Screen and ball-mill (12+ hours) to remove contamination
Reduce slurry water and increase specific gravity toward ~1.8 for denser laydown
For once-fired ware: switch to bisque firing, or use a fast-fire glaze with a soak

cross_reference.note: To deliberately induce (for testing): dampen the bisque ware before applying glaze. To fix: soak (hold at peak temperature) for 15-30 minutes at the end of firing.

blistering.summary: Larger ruptured bubbles in the fired surface; related to pinholing but driven more by melt rheology than raw gas volume.
causes: Insufficient melt fluidity to heal bubble ruptures
Paradoxically, a fluid melt with high surface tension can also trap bubbles (common in reactive high-boron glazes)
Excessive gas generation from dolomite, whiting, manganese dioxide, or other carbonates
Body gassing (from organics, up to ~950C) escaping through an already-melted glaze
High boron (0.7+ molar at cone 6) causing phase separation into glass regions of differing surface tension - these often blister worse on a refire
remedies: Reformulate for more fluidity: more flux, or a lower Al2O3:SiO2 ratio
Use a drop-and-hold schedule - cool to a lower, higher-viscosity temperature where bubbles break but the melt still levels
Substitute frits/wollastonite/cleaner clays for high-gas carbonates
Use a fast-fire glaze formulation that stays unmelted until after ~950C
Reduce boron; expect worse blistering on any refire of a high-boron glaze
Fire bisque hot (cone 04-02) and slow through 700-950C (50C/hr is 'slow')
Apply thinner; raise slurry specific gravity toward 1.8; ball-mill up to 12 hours
In gas kilns: avoid heavy reduction, start reduction 1-2 cones above bisque temperature, avoid flame impingement

cross_reference.note: To deliberately induce (for testing): add 2% silicon carbide and 5% titanium dioxide to a matte glaze or underlying slip. To avoid: fire to a lower temperature, or apply the glaze more thinly.

dunting_cracking.summary: Cracks from thermal stress during firing or cooling, distinct from drying cracks.
causes: Temperature gradients within a piece from uneven heating or cooling
Cooling (or heating) too fast through the quartz inversion point (~1050F / 570C)
Thick, uneven wall sections; sharp concave angles that concentrate stress
Wide flat bottoms absorbing heat unevenly from kiln shelves
Rapid heat-up rate amplifying existing gradients in thick or irregular pieces
remedies: Slow the firing cycle through quartz inversion in both directions, especially cooling
Extended low-temperature holds to remove moisture gradually
Round and compress sharp concave angles; aim for even wall thickness
Ensure even kiln heat distribution; electric kilns need slower firing (no draft to even things out)
Overnight candling at the boiling point before ramping up

bittiness.summary: Small imperfections make the fired glaze surface look and feel slightly rough, despite adequate glaze thickness over the body.
causes: Glaze not sieved, or sieved through too coarse a mesh, or a faulty sieve
Material added to the glaze after sieving
Contamination from material clinging to the clay/bisque surface, dislodged during dipping

Crystals of calcium carbonate growing in stored slop glaze - frits have a small but real solubility in water, and dissolved calcium recombines with carbonate ions from dissolved CO2 in the water over time (worse in warm weather, worse with more soluble/alkaline frits)
remedies: Resieve the glaze through a sufficiently fine mesh; fit a recirculation pump to keep glaze in suspension and continuously screened
Store slop glaze cool - calcium carbonate crystal growth is markedly slower in cold storage
Store glaze dry rather than as a slop where practical
Reformulate toward stiffer, less soluble frits if recurring
A small acid addition (hydrochloric or acetic) delays carbonate bead formation, but flocculates the glaze - usually not worth the tradeoff

cross_reference.note: Removing the tiny calcium carbonate beads before use does not measurably change the fired glaze, since the calcium removed is a small fraction of the total.

bloating.summary: Bulges or blisters appear in ware fired to vitrification (stoneware/porcelain), revealing a cavity when broken open. Rare in porous bodies like earthenware.
bloating.chemistry_cause: Gas generation (from carbonaceous material burning off, or dissociation of iron oxides/sulphides/carbonates/manganese) coinciding with vitrification sealing the body's surface before the gas can escape.
causes: Overfiring, or firing too quickly through the 650-1000C carbon-burnout range before the surface vitrifies
Increased volatile/carbonaceous material content in the clay batch (fireclays and ball clays can vary 1-2% batch to batch)
Residual moisture in once-fired ware at the point the surface densifies, trapping interior gas
Reduction within the 650-1000C range converts Fe2O3 to FeO, a much more vigorous flux that seals the surface early
More common in electric kilns (poor ventilation vs. a gas kiln's moving atmosphere) and in tightly packed loads
remedies: Lower the maximum firing temperature (treats the symptom, not the cause, but usually works)
Slow the firing through the 650-1000C carbon-burnout range, or extend once-fired ware's time in that range to 5+ hours
Add grog or coarse sand to open the body structure and let gases escape more easily
Use low-iron clays/grogs if firing in reduction, since high-iron material fluxes and softens early, allowing easier deformation
Ensure ware is fully dry before firing, or slow the firing to compensate for residual moisture
To diagnose: refire some unglazed ware from the same load - if it stays bloat-free while glazed ware bloats, the cause is trapped gas rather than overfiring

cross_reference.note: Electric kilns bloat more readily than gas due to poorer ventilation during the carbon-burnout stage.

blow_out.summary: A piece of biscuit or glazed biscuit flakes/ejects away from the pot, usually during biscuit firing, leaving a cavity - often with a white or off-white particle remnant visible at its base.
causes: Particles of pyrites or lime-bearing nodules in the clay, which hydrate and swell after a low-temperature biscuit firing
With once-fired (not twice-fired) ware, pyrite particles can eject pieces of ware directly
remedies: Source clay with fewer mineral inclusions, or screen/process to remove them

Lime blow-outs are rare in stoneware/porcelain: the higher firing temperature converts the lime nodule into stable complex silicates instead of reverting to reactive calcium oxide on cooling, and the fired body is strong enough to resist the hydration pressure

cross_reference.note: Distinct from bloating: blow-out is a biscuit-stage mineral-inclusion problem, not a glost-stage gas-trapping problem.

colemanite_splutter.summary: Pieces of glaze are ejected from the pot during firing when colemanite releases its water of crystallisation too quickly (colemanite is ~27% water by weight, typically released 400-800C) - leaves bare patches on the ware and glaze speckles on the kiln shelf.
colemanite_splutter.chemistry_cause: Colemanite (hydrated calcium borate, ~2CaO*3B2O3*5H2O, composition varies by source) is a variable, partly-soluble natural mineral - unlike a fritted boron source, its water of crystallisation is released raw during firing rather than already driven off during manufacture.
causes: Too much colemanite in the recipe relative to what the glaze film thickness can tolerate
European (Turkish) colemanite splutters more readily than American sources at the same percentage
chemistry_remedies: Replace colemanite with calcium borate frit (an exact drop-in for the boron/calcium chemistry, with the water already removed during fritting) - the standard industry fix
Keep raw colemanite to roughly 7-10% of the recipe for European sources if it must be used raw (American colemanite tolerates somewhat more)
other_remedies: Fire more slowly up to about 800C
Keep the glaze film as thin as possible

cross_reference.note: Gerstley Borate behaves similarly - it's an ore containing colemanite plus ulexite (sodium calcium borate).
